subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In typography, what are 'serifs'?
options: The small strokes or feet at the ends of letterforms
The overall spacing between lines of text
The measurement unit used for type size
The empty space around a block of text
questions.explain: Serifs are the small finishing strokes at the ends of letters; typefaces without them are called sans-serif.

questions.q: Which typographic term describes adjusting the space between two individual letters?
options: Kerning
Leading
Weight
Alignment
questions.explain: Kerning is the adjustment of space between specific pairs of letters to improve their visual fit.

questions.q: What does 'leading' control in a piece of typographic layout?
options: The vertical space between lines of text
The space between two adjacent letters
The thickness of the letter strokes
The colour contrast of the text
questions.explain: Leading (line spacing) sets the vertical distance between baselines, affecting readability and density.

questions.q: Why do designers create a typographic hierarchy in a layout?
options: To guide the reader's eye and show the order of importance of information
To reduce the number of colours used on the page
To make all text the same size for consistency
To ensure the design can only be printed in CMYK
questions.explain: Varying size, weight and position creates hierarchy so viewers read the most important content first.

questions.q: You are designing a gig poster and want the band's name to be seen first. Which is the most effective typographic approach?
options: Set the band's name in a much larger, bolder type than the other details
Set every element in the same size and weight
Place the band's name in small text at the bottom
Use a very pale colour for the band's name
questions.explain: Increased size and weight establish hierarchy, drawing the eye to the most important element first.

questions.q: In the CMYK colour model used for print, what does the 'K' stand for?
options: Key (black)
Khaki
Kelvin
Kilo
questions.explain: CMYK stands for Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Key (black), the four inks used in standard colour printing.

questions.q: Which colour model should a designer work in when creating graphics intended to be viewed on screens?
options: RGB
CMYK
Pantone spot colours
Greyscale
questions.explain: Screens emit light and mix Red, Green and Blue additively, so digital work is created in RGB.

questions.q: Complementary colours are those which are:
options: Positioned opposite each other on the colour wheel
Positioned next to each other on the colour wheel
All warm in temperature
Different tints of the same hue
questions.explain: Complementary colours sit opposite on the colour wheel and create strong contrast when paired.

questions.q: A client wants packaging that feels calm and relaxing for a spa brand. Which colour choice best supports this?
options: A palette of cool blues and greens
A palette of bright reds and oranges
High-contrast black and yellow
Vivid clashing neon colours
questions.explain: Cool colours such as blue and green are generally associated with calmness and relaxation.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of using a grid in a graphic layout?
options: To organise and align elements consistently across the design
To force every image to be square
To limit the design to a single colour
To remove all white space from the page
questions.explain: Grids provide structure, helping designers align text and images for a coherent, organised layout.

questions.q: In layout, what is 'white space' (also called negative space)?
options: The empty area around and between elements that aids clarity and focus
Any area that must be printed in white ink
A mistake caused by leaving out content
The space reserved only for a logo
questions.explain: White space is the intentional empty area that prevents clutter and helps guide the viewer's attention.

questions.q: How are vector graphics constructed?
options: From paths defined by mathematical equations
From a grid of individual coloured pixels
From layers of scanned photographs only
From randomly generated dots
questions.explain: Vectors use mathematically defined points and paths, so they can be scaled to any size without losing quality.

questions.q: What typically happens when a low-resolution raster (bitmap) image is enlarged significantly?
options: It becomes blurred or pixelated and loses quality
It stays perfectly sharp at any size
It automatically converts into a vector
It changes colour mode to CMYK
questions.explain: Raster images are made of a fixed number of pixels, so enlarging them stretches the pixels and reduces quality.

questions.q: Which piece of Adobe software is primarily vector-based and suited to creating logos and illustrations?
options: Adobe Illustrator
Adobe Photoshop
Adobe Lightroom
Adobe Audition
questions.explain: Illustrator works with vectors, whereas Photoshop is primarily a raster (pixel) editing program.

questions.q: What resolution is generally recommended for high-quality printed graphics?
options: 300 dpi
72 dpi
10 dpi
1000 dpi
questions.explain: Print work is normally prepared at around 300 dots per inch, while 72 dpi is typical for screen use.

questions.q: A logo must appear crisp on both a business card and a large billboard. Which file type is most suitable?
options: A vector file
A low-resolution JPEG
A 72 dpi bitmap
An animated GIF
questions.explain: Vectors scale to any size without loss of quality, making them ideal for logos used at very different sizes.

questions.q: In graphic communication, what is a logo?
options: A graphic symbol or mark used to identify and represent a brand
A block of body text on a page
The grid used to lay out a poster
The printing process used for packaging
questions.explain: A logo is a distinctive mark that identifies an organisation or product and supports its brand identity.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'target audience' of a graphic design?
options: The specific group of people the design is intended to reach
The printer who produces the final artwork
The colour palette chosen for the design
The software used to create the artwork
questions.explain: Identifying the target audience helps a designer make choices suited to who will view the work.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a mood board in a graphic design project?
options: To gather visual references and ideas that inform the direction of a design
To calculate the final printing cost
To replace the need for any sketches
To measure the resolution of images
questions.explain: A mood board collects imagery, colours and type samples to explore and communicate a design's visual direction.

questions.q: You are designing packaging for a children's breakfast cereal. Which approach best communicates the message to the audience?
options: Bright, playful colours with fun illustrated characters
Muted greys with dense small print
A formal serif layout with no imagery
A minimal monochrome corporate style
questions.explain: Lively colours and friendly characters suit a young audience and clearly communicate a fun, appealing product.
